{"id": "0e220d38-74bd-4028-9836-ddaea1f3c8b8", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_eG9cYz7lekG5EM2GGc6LJd", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"AWS Direct Connect as Primary and AWS Site-to-Site VPN as Backup\",\"context\":\"## AWS Direct Connect primary and VPN backup architecture\\n\\nThe following steps describe the on-premises to AWS traffic flow:\\n\\n1. Traffic from the office branch destined to the **Spoke VPC B** is forwarded to the Transit Gateway through the AWS Direct Connect link. This behavior can be achieved by configuring the office branch devices with higher BGP local preference pointing to the DX peer. The Transit Gateway is connected to Direct Connect by using a Transit VIF and a Direct Connect Gateway.\\n2. As per the **Transit Gateway on-premises route table**, the traffic is forwarded to the **spoke VPC B** attachment.\\n3. The TGW ENI of the **spoke VPC B** forwards the traffic to the destination.\\n\\nIn the event of an AWS Direct Connect failure:\\n\\n1. Traffic from the office branch destined to the **spoke VPC B** is forwarded to the Transit Gateway through the AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection.\\n2. As per the **Transit Gateway on-premises route table**, the traffic is forwarded to the **spoke VPC B** attachment.\\n3. The TGW ENI of the **spoke VPC B** forwards the traffic to the destination.\\n\\nFor more information about how to configure AWS Direct Connect with AWS Site-to-Site VPN as a backup, see Using a VPN connection as a backup to Direct Connect.\\n\\nFor more information about asymmetric routing, see Resolve asymmetric routing issues on AWS re:Post\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/reference-architecture-diagrams/latest/hybrid-connectivity-transit-gateway/hybrid-dx-primary-vpn-backup.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Reliability\",\"context\":\"## VPN connection as a backup to AWS DX connection example\\n\\nVPN can be selected to provide a backup network connection to an AWS Direct Connect\\nconnection. Typically, this type of connectivity model is driven by cost, because it\\nprovides a lower level of reliability to the overall hybrid connectivity solution due to\\nindeterministic performance over the internet, and there is no SLA that can be obtained for\\na connection over the public internet. It is a valid and cost-effective connectivity model,\\nand should be used when cost is the top priority consideration and there is a limited\\nbudget, or possibly as an interim solution until a secondary DX can be provisioned. Figure\\n12 illustrates the design of this connectivity model. One key consideration with this\\ndesign, where both the VPN and DX connections are terminating at the AWS Transit Gateway, is that\\nthe VPN connection can advertise higher number of routes compared to the ones that can be\\nadvertised over a DX connection connected to AWS Transit Gateway. This may cause a suboptimal\\nrouting situation. An option to resolve this issue is to configure route filtering at the\\ncustomer gateway device (CGW) for the routes received from the VPN connection, allowing only\\nthe summary routes to be accepted.\\n\\nNote: To create the summary route on the AWS Transit Gateway, you need to specify a static\\nroute to an arbitrary attachment in the AWS Transit Gateway route table so that the summary is sent\\nalong the more specific route.\\n\\nFrom the AWS Transit Gateway routing table\u2019s point of view, the routes for the on-premises\\nprefix are received both from the AWS DX connection (via DXGW) and from VPN, with the same\\nprefix length. Following the route\\npriority logic of AWS Transit Gateway, routes received over Direct Connect have a higher\\npreference than the ones received over Site-to-Site VPN, and thus the path over the AWS Direct Connect will\\nbe the preferred to reach the on-premises network(s).\\n\\n*Figure 12 \u2013 VPN connection as a backup to AWS DX connection example*\\n\\nThe following decision tree guides you through making the desired decision for\\nachieving a resilient (which will result in a reliably) hybrid network connectivity. For\\nmore information, refer to AWS Direct Connect Resiliency\\nToolkit.\\n\\n*Figure 13 \u2013 Reliability decision tree*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/hybrid-connectivity/reliability.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"directconnect\",\"skill_description\":\"Configures AWS Direct Connect: choosing a connection model (dedicated, hosted, or a link aggregation group) and completing the cross connect; creating private, public, and transit virtual interfaces and bringing up BGP; reaching many VPCs through a Direct Connect gateway including cross-account transit gateway associations; encrypting traffic with MACsec or a private IP Site-to-Site VPN; making the connection resilient and tuning failover; managing link aggregation groups; SiteLink; and migrating from a virtual private gateway to a transit gateway. Use when the user wants a private, consistent network link between a data center and AWS, or operates an existing Direct Connect setup and needs to extend, encrypt, or harden it. Routes to the right per-task procedure in references. Do NOT use for transit gateway route tables and attachments (transitgateway skill), Site-to-Site VPN without Direct Connect (sitetositevpn skill), or Route 53 DNS routing (route53 skill).\\n\\n\\nServices: directconnect, vpc, transitgateway\\nTasks: configure, secure, deploy\\nPersona: network-admin, devops, developer, sre\\nWorkload: networking, hybrid-cloud\\n*\",\"skill_name\":\"directconnect\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Check AWS doc on using Site-to-Site VPN as backup for Direct Connect failover behavior"}

{"id": "ca50bd7c-0bc3-4198-8c3f-d88386a4a28d", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "This confirms exactly what you'd expect: with equal prefix length, **AWS always prefers the Direct Connect path over the VPN path** to the VGW — this is a hard-coded AWS routing preference, not something you configure via local preference or AS_PATH on the AWS side. You don't need to (and can't) tune AWS's inbound preference between the two; DX wins automatically whenever it's up and advertising the same or a more specific prefix.

Where asymmetric routing actually creeps in is almost always on **your side** — the path AWS picks outbound (DX, by default) doesn't match the path your on-prem network picks inbound toward AWS. A few concrete causes and fixes:

**Causes**
- Your on-prem/CGW router doesn't give DX a clear preference, so return traffic (toward AWS) sometimes goes out the VPN while traffic from AWS comes back over DX, or vice versa.
- The VPN connection advertises a longer/more specific prefix than DX (longest-prefix-match always wins regardless of local preference), accidentally making VPN the active path for some subnets.
- Stateful devices (firewalls, NAT) on-prem seeing only one leg of a flow and dropping it because the return path differs.

**How to keep it symmetric**
1. **Match prefix granularity on both paths.** Advertise the *same* prefixes (same length) over DX and VPN. Don't let the VPN side get more specific — that silently overrides AWS's DX preference via longest-prefix-match.
2. **Set local preference on your on-prem BGP routers** so outbound (on-prem → AWS) traffic also prefers the path reachable via DX, mirroring AWS's own preference inbound. Since AWS already prefers DX automatically, aligning your CGW to do the same keeps both directions on DX.
3. **Use consistent AS_PATH length** for the same prefix on both circuits if you're not using local preference, since AS_PATH is the next tiebreaker after local preference.
4. If you're running this through a Transit Gateway rather than directly at the VGW, apply route filtering on the CGW so the VPN only advertises summary routes — otherwise VPN's more specific routes can win on longest-prefix-match even with DX up.
5. Avoid flow-breaking stateful devices across the two paths, or make sure they can tolerate asymmetric return traffic during failover.
